What is the smallest number of jumps the kangaroo must make to move from its current position to position $\mathrm{A}$ ?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached image shows a checkerboard with the kangaroo on its current square near the center. Arrows from that square illustrate the legal kangaroo jumps: either 3 squares in one direction and 1 square perpendicular to it. The target square labeled A is diagonally adjacent to the kangaroo's current square, one column to the right and one row downward. Reasoning: Let the current square be (0,0), with x positive to the right and y positive upward. Then A has displacement (1,-1). A legal jump has vector (±3,±1) or (±1,±3). One jump cannot reach A, because (1,-1) is not a 3-and-1 move. Two jumps also cannot reach A: each jump changes both coordinates by odd numbers, so after two jumps both coordinate changes would be even, but (1,-1) has odd coordinate changes. A 3-jump route exists because (3,1)+(-3,1)+(1,-3)=(1,-1), and each vector is a legal kangaroo jump. Therefore the smallest possible number of jumps is 3.

From the text, each legal jump is one of (±3,±1) or (±1,±3). First show A cannot be reached in 1 jump because its displacement is not of type 3-and-1. It also cannot be reached in 2 jumps because every jump changes both coordinates by odd numbers, so after two jumps both coordinate changes would be even, while A differs from the start by odd changes in both coordinates. Then exhibit a 3-jump route whose vectors sum to the A displacement, for example (3,1)+(-3,1)+(1,-3)=(1,-1), choosing the corresponding up-right, up-left, then down-right jumps as shown by the allowed move pattern. Therefore the minimum is 3.

Using the text's move rule and the arrows, mark all squares reachable in exactly 1 jump; A is not among them. Next, from each of those marked squares, mark all legal second-jump destinations that remain on the board; check that A is still not marked. Finally, find that A is reached on the third layer, for instance by moving 3 right and 1 up, then 3 left and 1 up, then 1 right and 3 down, which lands on the square labeled A.
